title: Gastrulation and Embryonic Folding
summary: How a flat two-layer disc becomes a three-layer embryo with a head, tail, left and right.

lessons.title: The Primitive Streak and Primitive Node

levels.kid:
Early on, a baby starts as a tiny flat disc, a bit like a round pancake made of two thin layers. It is smaller than a grain of sand!

In the third week, a groove appears down the middle of the disc. It is called the **primitive streak**. It is like a line drawn on the pancake that shows which end will be the head and which will be the bottom. It also shows left and right.

At the head end of the line is a little bump called the **node**. Cells on the top layer crawl toward the line, slip down into it, and spread out underneath. This turns two layers into three. Every part of your body comes from those three layers!
levels.hs:
During the third week after fertilization, the embryo is a flat **bilaminar disc** with two layers: the **epiblast** (top) and the **hypoblast** (bottom). The process that turns this into three layers is called **gastrulation**, and it begins with the **primitive streak**.

The primitive streak is a thickened line of epiblast cells. It appears around day 15 at the future tail end and grows toward the future head. Down its middle runs a groove, the **primitive groove**. At the head end sits a raised knot of cells, the **primitive node** (Hensen's node), with a small dip called the **primitive pit**.

Why it matters:
- It sets up the **body axes**. The streak marks head-to-tail (cranial-caudal), back-to-front (dorsal-ventral), and left-right.
- It is the gateway for gastrulation. Epiblast cells move toward the streak, lose their tight connections, and dive through the groove. This inward movement is called **ingression**.
- Cells that go through form the **endoderm** (replacing the hypoblast) and the **mesoderm** (a new middle layer). Cells that stay on top become **ectoderm**.

A real example: if the streak does not shrink away on schedule, leftover cells near the tailbone can form a **sacrococcygeal teratoma**. This is the most common tumor in newborns.
levels.college:
Gastrulation converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar embryo. It starts around day 14 to 15 with the appearance of the **primitive streak** in the caudal midline of the epiblast.

**Formation.** Epiblast cells in the posterior region proliferate and converge toward the midline, forming a thickening that elongates cranially. Key structures:
- **Primitive groove**: a midline furrow along the streak.
- **Primitive node** (Hensen's node): an elevated cranial end surrounding the **primitive pit**.
- The streak defines the craniocaudal axis and makes bilateral symmetry explicit, so left and right sides now exist.

**Ingression.** Epiblast cells at the streak undergo an **epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)**:
- Downregulation of **E-cadherin**, driven by transcription factors such as **Snail**.
- Loss of apical-basal polarity, breakdown of the basement membrane, and acquisition of migratory behavior.
- FGF8 signaling from the streak represses E-cadherin and promotes migration.

The first ingressing cells displace the hypoblast to form **definitive endoderm**. Later cells spread between the layers as **intraembryonic mesoderm**. Remaining epiblast becomes **ectoderm**.

**Regional fate along the streak.** Position predicts destiny:
- Through the **node**: prechordal plate and **notochordal process** (axial mesoderm).
- Cranial streak: paraxial mesoderm (future somites).
- Mid-streak: intermediate mesoderm.
- Caudal streak: lateral plate and extraembryonic mesoderm.

**Organizer.** The node is the mammalian equivalent of Spemann's organizer. It secretes BMP antagonists (**chordin, noggin, follistatin**) that help specify dorsal and neural fates.

**Regression.** As the embryo grows, the streak shrinks relative to the embryo and retreats caudally. It normally vanishes by the end of week 4. Persistent remnants can give rise to **sacrococcygeal teratomas**, which contain tissues from all three germ layers.
levels.phd:
Primitive streak initiation depends on asymmetric signaling between embryonic and extraembryonic tissues. In the mouse, **Nodal** (a TGF-β family ligand) from the posterior epiblast, together with **Wnt3** and BMP4 from extraembryonic ectoderm, induces posterior identity. The **anterior visceral endoderm (AVE)** migrates anteriorly and secretes antagonists. **Lefty1** and **Cer1** inhibit Nodal, and **Dkk1** inhibits Wnt. This confines streak formation to the opposite, posterior pole. The **Brachyury (T)** gene, a T-box transcription factor, marks the streak and nascent mesoderm. Wnt3 knockouts and Nodal mutants fail to form a streak.

In the chick, which is best studied for cell movements, the streak forms by **polonaise movements**. These are bilateral counter-rotating flows of epiblast that converge at the posterior midline. They are driven by planar cell polarity-dependent intercalation and directional contractility, as shown by Voiculescu and Stern. Classic grafting by **Waddington** (1932–33) showed that the chick node and streak induce a secondary axis. **Beddington** (1994) showed the mouse node organizes an ectopic axis. Together these established the node as homologous to the amphibian **Spemann-Mangold organizer** (1924).

EMT at the streak involves **Snail1**-mediated E-cadherin repression, **FGF8**/FGFR1 signaling, and focal basement-membrane degradation. *Fgfr1* null cells accumulate in the streak, unable to leave. Fate is set by both timing and position. Fate maps by Lawson and by Tam show a **spatiotemporal colinearity**: cells ingressing earliest through the posterior streak form extraembryonic and lateral mesoderm, while later cells ingressing more anteriorly form paraxial and axial derivatives. Hox gene activation begins in the posterior streak and links ingression time to axial identity.

The node contains **neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs)** in the adjacent node-streak border and caudal lateral epiblast. These bipotent, Sox2+/T+ cells continue to generate both posterior neural tube and paraxial mesoderm, extending the trunk long after gastrulation proper. A long-standing debate is whether a discrete 'organizer' exists, or whether organizer activity is a distributed property of a signaling field. The fact that node ablation in mouse still permits substantial axis formation supports the field view.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the primitive streak matters most through its failures and its leftovers. Streak and node biology also underpin modern stem-cell and ethics frameworks.

**Sacrococcygeal teratoma (SCT).** SCT is the commonest neonatal tumor, at roughly 1 in 35,000–40,000 births, with a female predominance near 3–4:1. It is classically attributed to totipotent remnants of the regressing streak or node near the coccyx, though a primordial germ cell origin remains debated. Altman classification (types I–IV) grades how much of the tumor is external versus presacral. Large, highly vascular fetal SCTs can cause high-output cardiac failure and hydrops. Selected cases are managed with fetal intervention or an EXIT strategy. Complete coccygectomy is essential, because leaving the coccyx is associated with recurrence, including malignant yolk sac tumor. AFP serves as a surveillance marker.

**Caudal dysgenesis.** Defective caudal mesoderm production from the late streak and tail bud produces a spectrum of malformations. These range from sacral agenesis to **sirenomelia**, with fused lower limbs often accompanied by renal agenesis. Maternal diabetes is the strongest known risk factor for caudal regression. Currarino syndrome (*MNX1*) links sacral defects, presacral mass and anorectal malformation. These conditions overlap with the neurosurgical territory of tethered cord and occult spinal dysraphism.

**The 14-day rule.** Appearance of the streak is the biological landmark behind the internationally used limit on culturing human embryos. Streak formation signals the start of individuation, after which twinning becomes unlikely. In 2021 the ISSCR removed its blanket 14-day prohibition from its guidelines, recommending case-by-case review. This reopened debate as labs began approaching that limit.

**Stem-cell models.** Human **gastruloids** and stem-cell-based embryo models now recapitulate streak-like Brachyury expression, symmetry breaking and somitogenesis in vitro. Directed differentiation protocols mimic streak signaling to make definitive endoderm and mesoderm from pluripotent cells. For example, activin/Nodal plus Wnt activation (such as GSK3 inhibition) is used to make pancreatic, hepatic and cardiac lineages.

Open questions include how human streak dynamics differ from the mouse cup and the chick disc. The 2021 Tyser et al. single-cell atlas of a single human gastrula (Carnegie stage 7) is a key, though limited, reference.

keyPoints: The primitive streak appears around day 15 in the caudal midline of the epiblast
The streak sets up head-tail, back-front and left-right axes
The primitive node (Hensen's node) sits at the cranial end around the primitive pit
Epiblast cells undergo EMT and ingress to form endoderm and mesoderm
Position of ingression along the streak predicts mesoderm fate
Streak remnants can cause sacrococcygeal teratoma, the commonest newborn tumor

test.q: Which layer of the bilaminar disc forms the primitive streak?
test.explain: The streak is a thickening of epiblast cells. All three germ layers come from the epiblast; the hypoblast is displaced.

test.q: Where does the primitive streak first appear?
choices: At the center of the amnion
test.explain: It appears at the future tail end of the midline and elongates cranially.

test.q: The raised knot of cells at the cranial end of the streak is the:
test.explain: The primitive (Hensen's) node sits at the cranial end around the primitive pit.

test.q: Epiblast cells passing through the streak undergo a change called:
test.explain: EMT lets cells lose tight junctions and polarity so they can migrate inward. MET is the reverse process.

test.q: Downregulating which adhesion molecule helps cells leave the epiblast?
test.explain: Snail and FGF8 repress E-cadherin, loosening cell-cell adhesion so cells can ingress.

test.q: The first cells to ingress through the streak mainly form:
test.explain: Early ingressing cells displace the hypoblast to become definitive endoderm.

test.q: Cells passing through the caudal part of the streak mostly become:
test.explain: The caudal streak gives lateral plate and extraembryonic mesoderm. The node gives axial mesoderm, and the cranial streak gives paraxial mesoderm.

test.q: The mammalian node is considered equivalent to which amphibian structure?
test.explain: The node acts like the Spemann organizer at the dorsal blastopore lip and can induce a secondary axis.

test.q: Persistent primitive streak remnants are linked to which tumor?
test.explain: Leftover streak cells near the coccyx can form sacrococcygeal teratomas containing all three germ layers.

test.q: The process that turns the two-layer disc into three layers is called ___.
test.explain: Gastrulation begins with the primitive streak and produces ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

test.q: What is the small depression in the center of the primitive node called?
test.explain: The primitive pit lies within the node, continuous with the primitive groove.

test.q: The primitive node is also called ___'s node.
test.explain: It is named after Victor Hensen, who described it in the chick.

advancedTest.q: Why does the streak form at the posterior pole of the mouse epiblast rather than anteriorly?
choices: Brachyury is expressed first in the anterior visceral endoderm
The posterior epiblast lacks receptors for Nodal and Wnt ligands
BMP4 from the hypoblast directly represses posterior Snail expression
The AVE secretes Lefty1, Cer1 and Dkk1, suppressing streak signals anteriorly
advancedTest.explain: The migrating AVE antagonizes Nodal and Wnt anteriorly, restricting streak-inducing signals to the posterior pole.

advancedTest.q: Fgfr1-null cells pile up within the primitive streak. This suggests FGF signaling is needed for:
choices: Leaving the streak by completing EMT and migration
Regressing the node toward the caudal tail bud
Inducing Nodal expression in the posterior epiblast
Specifying epiblast pluripotency before streak formation
advancedTest.explain: Cells reach the streak but cannot exit, indicating FGF8/FGFR1 drives E-cadherin repression and migration away from the streak.

advancedTest.q: Which finding most supports viewing organizer activity as a distributed signaling field?
choices: Substantial axis formation persists after mouse node ablation
Chordin and noggin are both expressed in the node
Brachyury marks the streak and nascent mesoderm
Node grafts in the chick induce a complete secondary axis
advancedTest.explain: If axes still form without the node, organizer function must be shared by other tissues. Graft induction supports the node's capacity but not exclusivity.

advancedTest.q: Why does excising the coccyx matter in sacrococcygeal teratoma surgery?
choices: Retained coccyx is linked to recurrence, including yolk sac tumor
The coccyx is the site of maternal diabetic injury
The coccyx produces the AFP used for surveillance
Removing the coccyx prevents later caudal dysgenesis
advancedTest.explain: Totipotent remnants near the coccyx can persist; leaving it raises recurrence risk, sometimes malignant.

lessons.title: Ectoderm, Mesoderm and Endoderm: Germ Layer Fates

levels.kid:
Early on, a baby starts as a tiny flat disc, smaller than a grain of rice. Then the disc builds three layers, like a sandwich with three slices. Each layer has its own job.

- The **top layer (ectoderm)** makes the skin, hair, and the brain and nerves.
- The **middle layer (mesoderm)** makes muscles, bones, the heart and blood.
- The **inner layer (endoderm)** makes the lining of the tummy, the lungs and the liver.

Think of it like a team where everyone picks a job very early. A cell in the top layer usually grows up to be part of your skin or brain, not your stomach. These three layers build every part of your body.
levels.hs:
During week three of development, the embryo goes through **gastrulation**, the process that turns a two-layer disc into three **germ layers**. Cells from the top layer, the **epiblast**, move inward through a groove called the primitive streak. The first cells to go in replace the bottom layer and become **endoderm**. Cells that go in next settle in between as **mesoderm**. The cells that stay on top become **ectoderm**. So all three layers come from the epiblast.

What each layer becomes:
- **Ectoderm**: epidermis (outer skin), hair, nails, the brain and spinal cord, the lens of the eye, and tooth enamel.
- **Mesoderm**: skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle, bone, cartilage, the heart, blood and blood vessels, the kidneys, and the gonads.
- **Endoderm**: the inner lining of the gut tube, the lining of the lungs and airways, the liver, the pancreas, the thyroid, and the bladder lining.

A useful example is the intestine. Its inner lining, which absorbs food, comes from endoderm. The smooth muscle around it that squeezes food along comes from mesoderm. The nerves that control that squeezing come from ectoderm, through the neural crest. Most organs are built this way, with tissue from more than one layer.

A handy memory trick: ecto = outside, meso = middle, endo = inside.
levels.college:
Gastrulation (around days 15 to 21) converts the bilaminar disc into a trilaminar embryo. Epiblast cells undergo an **epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)** at the primitive streak, losing E-cadherin and gaining migratory behavior. They then ingress. The earliest ingressing cells displace the hypoblast to form **definitive endoderm**. Later cells spread laterally and cranially as **intraembryonic mesoderm**. The remaining epiblast becomes **ectoderm**. The hypoblast itself contributes mainly to extraembryonic tissues.

**Ectoderm** splits into three lineages:
- **Surface ectoderm**: epidermis, hair, nails, sweat and mammary glands, lens, inner ear epithelium (otic placode), enamel, anterior pituitary (Rathke's pouch).
- **Neuroectoderm** (neural tube): brain, spinal cord, retina, posterior pituitary, pineal gland.
- **Neural crest**: peripheral sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla chromaffin cells, and much of the facial skeleton and meninges.

**Mesoderm** is organized from medial to lateral:
- **Paraxial**: somites, which give vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis of the back.
- **Intermediate**: kidneys, ureters, gonads and genital ducts.
- **Lateral plate**: the somatic layer forms the body wall and limb skeleton. The splanchnic layer forms gut smooth muscle, the heart, blood and vessels.
- **Axial mesoderm** (notochord) is covered in its own lesson.

**Endoderm** forms the epithelial lining of the gut tube and its outgrowths: liver hepatocytes, pancreas, gallbladder, respiratory epithelium and alveoli, thyroid and parathyroid glands, thymus epithelium, tympanic cavity, and bladder and urethra epithelium.

A general rule: endoderm supplies the functional epithelium (the **parenchyma**) of internal organs. Mesoderm supplies the supporting connective tissue, muscle and vessels (the **stroma**). Ectoderm and neural crest supply innervation.
levels.phd:
Germ layer specification is set by signaling gradients across the streak. The order of ingression and the timing of exposure decide fate. High, sustained **Nodal** (a TGF-β ligand acting through SMAD2/3) specifies definitive endoderm. Lower Nodal combined with **BMP4** and **WNT3** drives mesoderm. Mouse genetics showed this clearly: Nodal-null embryos fail to form a streak, and graded reductions in Nodal selectively lose anterior endoderm first.

Core transcription factors:
- Endoderm: **SOX17**, **FOXA2**, GATA4/6. Sox17-null mice lack definitive gut endoderm.
- Mesoderm: **Brachyury (TBXT)**, MIXL1, then MESP1 for cardiac mesoderm and TBX6 for paraxial mesoderm.
- Ectoderm: SOX2 and OTX2. Neural versus epidermal fate depends on BMP levels. Under the classic **default model**, from Hemmati-Brivanlou and Melton in *Xenopus*, ectoderm becomes neural unless BMP signaling holds it as epidermis. Organizer-derived antagonists (noggin, chordin, follistatin) block BMP and allow neural fate. The neural plate border, at intermediate BMP with WNT and FGF, gives neural crest and placodes.

Mesoderm is patterned mediolaterally by a BMP4 gradient. High lateral BMP produces lateral plate. Lower BMP produces intermediate and paraxial mesoderm. Somites then form with a periodicity set by the HES7/Notch segmentation clock.

The idea of three strictly separate germ layers has nuances:
- **Neural crest** is so multipotent that it is often called a "fourth germ layer." It makes ectomesenchyme (cartilage, bone, dentin), which breaks the rule that skeletal tissue comes from mesoderm.
- **Neuromesodermal progenitors** (co-expressing SOX2 and T) in the tail bud give both the posterior neural tube and paraxial mesoderm. This means ectoderm and mesoderm are not fully separated in the caudal axis.
- Lineage tracing shows that gut endoderm includes visceral endoderm cells (extraembryonic, hypoblast-derived) that become mixed into the definitive layer. In mouse, definitive endoderm does not fully replace the hypoblast lineage.

Germ layer identity is therefore a useful classification, not an absolute lineage barrier.
levels.expert:
Germ layer origin has practical uses in diagnosis, surgery and regenerative medicine.

**Tumor pathology.** Teratomas arise from pluripotent germ cells and contain tissues from all three layers, such as skin and hair, cartilage and bone, and gut or respiratory epithelium. Showing all three layers is the formal test of pluripotency for human iPSC and ESC lines. In vivo teratoma assays are increasingly being replaced by in vitro trilineage differentiation and scorecard gene panels (for example, ScoreCard-style qPCR). Immature teratoma grading depends on the amount of immature neuroectoderm, which is directly relevant to neuro-oncology.

**Neural crest disorders (neurocristopathies).** Hirschsprung disease (absent enteric ganglia, often linked to RET), neuroblastoma, DiGeorge-spectrum conotruncal and craniofacial defects, Waardenburg syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1 all reflect one shared lineage. Recognizing that lineage explains why defects that seem unrelated appear together in a single patient.

**Surgical anatomy.** Lineage predicts tissue behavior and blood supply. For neurosurgeons:
- The meninges of the forebrain come from neural crest, while caudal meninges come from mesoderm.
- The anterior pituitary (surface ectoderm) and posterior pituitary (neuroectoderm) have different origins. This explains why craniopharyngiomas, which arise from Rathke's pouch remnants, behave differently from neurohypophyseal lesions.

**Directed differentiation.** Protocols copy the embryo's signals. High Activin A, used as a Nodal stand-in, produces SOX17+/FOXA2+ definitive endoderm, which is then steered toward pancreatic beta cells. Stem-cell-derived islets have entered human trials for type 1 diabetes, including Vertex's zimislecel (VX-880). Dual-SMAD inhibition (blocking both BMP and TGF-β/Activin) converts pluripotent cells efficiently to neuroectoderm, which underlies dopaminergic neuron trials for Parkinson's disease.

**Pitfalls and open questions.**
- Markers overlap. Brachyury is expressed in neuromesodermal progenitors, and SOX17 also marks vascular endothelium. A single marker should not be used to assign a lineage.
- Human gastrulation can only be studied directly at limited stages, such as the Carnegie stage 7 embryo sequenced by Tyser and colleagues in 2021. Stem-cell embryo models, including gastruloids and somitoids, help fill the gap, but how faithful they are remains debated.
- Regulators still argue over whether to extend the 14-day rule for embryo culture, a limit that sits at the very start of gastrulation.

keyPoints: Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, all from the epiblast
First ingressing cells form endoderm, later cells mesoderm, cells that stay on top ectoderm
Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, and neural crest derivatives
Mesoderm: muscle, bone, heart, blood, kidneys, gonads
Endoderm: lining of the gut and airways, liver, pancreas, thyroid
High Nodal favors endoderm; low BMP lets ectoderm become neural

test.q: All three germ layers of the embryo proper are derived from which layer?
test.explain: Epiblast cells form endoderm, mesoderm and ectoderm. The hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic tissues.

test.q: Which structure is derived from ectoderm?
test.explain: The spinal cord comes from neuroectoderm. Hepatocytes are endodermal; heart muscle and kidneys are mesodermal.

test.explain: Intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the urogenital system.

Most organs combine tissue from several layers
Each organ comes from a single germ layer
Ectoderm forms the lining of the gut
test.explain: Most organs mix layers: for example, endodermal parenchyma, mesodermal stroma and ectoderm-derived nerves.

test.q: The process that converts the two-layer disc into three layers is called ___.
test.explain: Gastrulation occurs during week three.

test.q: Which germ layer forms the epidermis and the lens of the eye?
test.explain: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, lens, enamel and the anterior pituitary.

test.q: The first epiblast cells to ingress displace the hypoblast and become definitive ___.
test.explain: Early-ingressing cells form endoderm; later cells form mesoderm.

kidTest.q: How many germ layers does the early embryo make?
kidTest.explain: Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm make three layers.

kidTest.q: Which layer makes your brain and skin?
kidTest.explain: The top layer, called ectoderm, makes skin and nerves.

kidTest.q: Which layer makes your muscles and bones?
kidTest.explain: The middle layer, called mesoderm, builds muscle, bone, the heart and blood.

kidTest.q: What does the inner layer make?
kidTest.explain: The inner layer, called endoderm, lines the gut and makes the lungs and liver.

advancedTest.q: Graded reduction of Nodal signaling in mouse embryos would most likely cause:
choices: Loss of the somites with normal endoderm
Expanded anterior endoderm with too little mesoderm
Selective loss of anterior endoderm before other lineages
Conversion of the neural plate into epidermis
advancedTest.explain: Endoderm, especially anterior endoderm, needs the highest and most sustained Nodal, so it is lost first.

advancedTest.q: Under the default model, isolated ectoderm cells cultured without BMP would tend to become:
advancedTest.explain: BMP holds ectoderm in an epidermal state. Without BMP, ectoderm adopts a neural fate by default.

advancedTest.q: Why does neural crest challenge the strict three-layer scheme?
choices: It first appears after birth from adult stem cells
It arises from endoderm but later forms neurons
It forms skeletal tissue despite ectodermal origin
It forms the notochord and somites directly
advancedTest.explain: Neural crest ectomesenchyme makes cartilage, bone and dentin, tissues classically attributed to mesoderm.

advancedTest.q: A lab assigns definitive endoderm identity from SOX17 staining alone. The main risk is:
choices: SOX17 is restricted to the ectoderm
SOX17 mainly marks neural crest derivatives
SOX17 is missing from most endoderm
advancedTest.explain: Markers overlap: SOX17 is also expressed in endothelium, so lineage calls need several markers, such as FOXA2 together with SOX17.

lessons.title: Notochord Formation and Its Signaling Role

levels.kid:
Very early on, a baby is just a tiny flat disc of cells. Down the middle of that disc, a thin rod of cells grows. It is called the **notochord**.

Think of the notochord like a coach standing in the middle of a field. It shouts messages to the cells around it: "You become the brain and spinal cord!" "You become backbone!" The messages are special chemicals that spread out from the rod.

The notochord also makes the little embryo a bit stiffer, like a straw inside a jelly.

Later, most of the notochord goes away. A tiny bit stays as the soft squishy middle of the cushions between your backbones. So a piece of your very first coach is still inside you!
levels.hs:
The **notochord** is a flexible rod of cells that forms along the midline of the embryo during the third week of development. It defines the body's long axis, and it is the feature that gives our animal group, the **chordates**, its name.

The notochord comes from cells that move in through the **primitive node**, a small knot of cells at the front end of the primitive streak. These cells travel toward the head end in the midline, between the ectoderm above and the endoderm below.

Its most important job is **signaling**. The notochord releases a protein called **Sonic hedgehog (SHH)**. Cells receive SHH as a **morphogen**: a signal whose concentration tells cells what to become.
- Above it, SHH and other signals help the ectoderm form the **neural plate**, which becomes the brain and spinal cord.
- SHH tells nearby blocks of mesoderm, called **somites**, to make **sclerotome**, the cells that build the vertebrae.

After it has done its job, the notochord mostly disappears. Its remnants become the **nucleus pulposus**, the jelly-like center of each intervertebral disc. In adults, a herniated ("slipped") disc is this soft center pushing out, and it can press on a spinal nerve. So the notochord matters to spine surgeons long after birth.
levels.college:
**Formation.** Around days 16-17, epiblast cells that move in through the **primitive node** migrate cranially in the midline as the **notochordal (head) process**. They stop at the **prechordal plate**, which lies just caudal to the **oropharyngeal membrane**. Formation proceeds in steps:
- The head process hollows out to form the **notochordal canal**.
- The floor of this canal fuses with the underlying endoderm and then breaks down, producing the **notochordal plate**. For a short time the **neurenteric canal** connects the amniotic cavity to the yolk sac.
- The plate then folds off the endoderm and rolls up into a solid rod, the **definitive notochord**. Endoderm closes again beneath it.

**Signaling.** The notochord acts as an organizer for midline structures:
- **Neural induction:** it secretes BMP antagonists, **chordin**, **noggin** and **follistatin**. These block BMP4 so the overlying ectoderm takes a neural fate.
- **Floor plate induction:** notochord SHH induces the **floor plate** of the neural tube, which then makes its own SHH.
- **Ventral patterning:** an SHH gradient, high ventrally and low dorsally, sets up progenitor domains. These give **motor neurons** and ventral interneurons. Dorsal BMP/Wnt signals from the roof plate oppose it.
- **Sclerotome:** SHH, together with noggin, induces ventromedial somite cells to express **Pax1/Pax9** and become sclerotome, which forms the vertebral bodies around the notochord.

**Fate.** As the vertebral bodies form, notochord cells are squeezed out of them and collect in the intervertebral spaces. There they form the **nucleus pulposus**. A key transcription factor in notochord cells is **brachyury (TBXT)**, which is also a marker for notochord-derived tumors.
levels.phd:
**Lineage and morphogenesis.** Axial mesoderm arises from the node and from the anterior primitive streak. Fate mapping in mouse shows three contributions: an anterior head process, a trunk notochord from the node, and a tail notochord from the chordoneural hinge. Specification requires **Foxa2** and **brachyury (T/TBXT)**. Mouse *T* mutants lack a posterior notochord and die with axial truncation. In humans, the transient **intercalation** of notochordal cells into the endoderm (the notochordal plate stage) is distinctive. It is far less obvious in chick and is debated in mouse. Its persistence explains the human neurenteric canal.

**Organizer function.** Spemann and Mangold's 1924 grafts of the amphibian dorsal lip showed that axial mesoderm induces a secondary neural axis. Its molecular basis was identified in the 1990s as BMP antagonism (chordin, noggin, follistatin). This supported the "default model" of neural induction. Amniote data, however, show that FGF signaling and earlier Wnt inhibition also contribute. So BMP blockade is necessary but not sufficient.

**SHH morphogen.** SHH is cholesterol-modified and palmitoylated, and is released with the help of **Dispatched** and **Scube2**. It binds **Patched1**, relieving inhibition of **Smoothened**. This shifts **Gli** proteins from repressor (Gli3R) toward activator (Gli2A) forms. Work from the Jessell, Ericson and Briscoe labs showed that graded SHH exposure, read out by both concentration *and duration*, sets ventral progenitor domains (p3, pMN, p2, p1, p0). Cross-repressive homeodomain factors such as Nkx2.2 and Pax6, or Olig2 and Irx3, then sharpen these domains into sharp boundaries. Notochord ablation abolishes the floor plate and motor neurons, and ectopic notochord grafts induce extra ones (Placzek, Yamada et al.).

**Mechanical role.** Notochord cells contain large vacuoles that pressurize the rod. They are wrapped in a laminin/collagen sheath, so the notochord acts as a hydrostatic skeleton. In zebrafish, disrupting vacuoles shortens the axis and kinks the spine.

**Fate controversy.** Lineage tracing using *Shh-cre* in mouse established that nucleus pulposus cells are notochord-derived. In humans, notochordal-like cells decline in childhood and are replaced by chondrocyte-like cells. Whether these replacements descend from the notochord or invade from elsewhere remains disputed.
levels.expert:
**Chordoma.** Ectopic notochordal remnants can give rise to **chordoma**, a rare, slow-growing but locally aggressive bone tumor. It occurs mainly at the clivus and in the sacrococcygeal region, the two ends of the former axis. These are core skull-base and spine neurosurgical lesions. **Brachyury** nuclear staining is the diagnostic immunohistochemical marker, and it separates chordoma from chondrosarcoma. Germline *TBXT* duplication causes familial chordoma, and a common *TBXT* variant (rs2305089) is strongly associated with sporadic disease. Treatment centers on maximal en bloc or gross-total resection followed by high-dose proton or carbon-ion radiotherapy, because the tumor resists conventional chemotherapy. Research is targeting brachyury itself, for example with vaccines and CDK7/9 inhibition, which lowers TBXT transcription. **Benign notochordal cell tumors** in vertebrae can mimic chordoma on MRI. They lack bone destruction and soft-tissue mass, and confusing the two is a recognized pitfall. **Ecchordosis physaliphora**, a small retroclival remnant, is usually incidental.

**Split notochord and neurenteric malformations.** If the notochordal plate stage is abnormal, persistent contact between endoderm and ectoderm may result. This is thought to underlie **neurenteric cysts**, which are intraspinal cysts lined by endodermal epithelium. It may also underlie some **split cord malformations** (diastematomyelia) and the split notochord syndrome. These lesions are relevant to pediatric spine surgery.

**SHH and disease.** Too little SHH pathway signaling causes **holoprosencephaly**. Here the prechordal plate and ventral midline fail, and failure ranges from a single forebrain ventricle to midline facial defects. Teratogenic Smoothened antagonists such as cyclopamine illustrate the same pathway. Too much pathway activity drives **SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma** and basal cell carcinoma. Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib target it, but they carry fetal risk and can damage growth plates in children. The pathway is a striking example of a developmental morphogen becoming an oncology target.

**Disc regeneration.** Loss of notochordal cells parallels the start of disc degeneration. This has motivated studies of notochordal-cell-conditioned media and of iPSC-derived notochord-like cells, which are induced via TBXT/FOXA2 programs, as cell therapies for nucleus pulposus repair. Open questions are durability, the hypoxic nutrient-poor niche, and immunogenicity. Stem-cell-based **somitoids** and **axioloids** now recreate notochord-somite signaling in vitro and offer human-specific models.

keyPoints: Notochord forms from cells migrating cranially from the primitive node in week 3
It passes through head process, notochordal canal and plate stages to a solid rod
BMP antagonists (chordin, noggin, follistatin) help induce neural tissue
Notochord SHH induces the floor plate and patterns the ventral neural tube
SHH plus noggin induce sclerotome, which builds vertebrae
Remnants form the nucleus pulposus; ectopic remnants can cause chordoma

test.q: From which structure do the cells that form the notochord migrate?
test.explain: Notochordal cells move in through the primitive node and migrate cranially in the midline.

test.q: Which secreted protein from the notochord induces the floor plate of the neural tube?
test.explain: Notochord SHH induces the floor plate. BMP4 acts dorsally and opposes ventral fates.

test.q: How do chordin and noggin promote neural tissue formation?
choices: They activate Wnt signaling in ectoderm
They block BMP signaling in ectoderm
They degrade retinoic acid in the streak
They activate Patched in somite cells
test.explain: They are BMP antagonists. Blocking BMP4 lets the overlying ectoderm take a neural fate.

test.q: In the adult, notochord remnants persist as the:
test.explain: Notochord cells are squeezed into the intervertebral spaces and form the nucleus pulposus. The annulus fibrosus comes from sclerotome.

test.q: Which somite compartment does notochord SHH induce?
test.explain: SHH with noggin induces Pax1/Pax9-expressing sclerotome, which forms the vertebrae.

test.q: Ventral motor neurons arise where neural progenitors receive:
test.explain: Ventral fates such as motor neurons need high SHH. Dorsal BMP and Wnt signals oppose them.

test.q: The notochordal process extends cranially until it reaches the:
test.explain: It stops at the prechordal plate, just caudal to the oropharyngeal membrane.

test.q: The temporary neurenteric canal connects the amniotic cavity with the:
test.explain: During the notochordal plate stage, the neurenteric canal briefly links the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.

test.q: Which tumor arises from notochordal remnants?
test.explain: Chordoma arises from notochord remnants, mostly at the clivus and sacrum. Meningioma comes from the meninges.

test.q: Name the T-box transcription factor that marks notochord cells and chordomas.
test.explain: Brachyury (TBXT) is needed for the notochord and is the diagnostic stain for chordoma.

test.q: A signal whose concentration tells cells which fate to adopt is called a ___.
test.explain: SHH acts as a morphogen: different levels lead to different ventral cell fates.

test.q: Animals that have a notochord at some stage belong to which group?
test.explain: The notochord gives the chordates their name.

kidTest.q: Where does the notochord grow in the early embryo?
kidTest.explain: It forms as a thin rod down the middle of the embryo.

kidTest.q: How does the notochord tell other cells what to become?
kidTest.explain: It sends chemical messages that spread to nearby cells.

kidTest.q: The notochord helps cells become the brain, spinal cord and what else?
kidTest.explain: Its messages help build the backbone.

kidTest.q: Where is a bit of the notochord found in grown-ups?
choices: In the tips of the toenails
In the hair on top of the head
kidTest.explain: It stays as the soft middle of the cushions (discs) between backbones.

kidTest.q: The notochord acts like a c _ _ _ _ in the middle of the field.
kidTest.explain: Like a coach, it gives instructions to the cells around it.

advancedTest.q: A notochord grafted beside the dorsal neural tube would most likely produce:
choices: Loss of the somites on the side of the graft
Conversion of nearby ectoderm into endoderm
An extra floor plate and extra motor neurons
Extra roof plate tissue and dorsal sensory neurons
advancedTest.explain: Ectopic notochord SHH induces floor plate and ventral fates, including motor neurons, as the grafting experiments showed.

advancedTest.q: Amniote embryos argue against a pure 'default model' of neural induction because:
choices: BMP antagonists are absent from amniote embryos
Neural tissue arises solely from the endoderm
The notochord makes BMP4 instead of chordin
FGF and earlier Wnt inhibition are also required
advancedTest.explain: BMP blockade is necessary, but FGF signaling and earlier Wnt inhibition also contribute. So BMP blockade alone is not sufficient.

advancedTest.q: Why do clear progenitor boundaries form despite a smooth SHH gradient?
choices: Each neuron makes its own SHH at a fixed level
BMP from the floor plate reinforces each boundary
SHH spreads in sharp steps rather than a smooth gradient
Cross-repressive transcription factors sharpen the domains
advancedTest.explain: Pairs such as Nkx2.2 and Pax6, or Olig2 and Irx3, repress each other. This turns graded input into sharp domains.

advancedTest.q: A clival mass with nuclear brachyury staining is best explained by:
choices: A cartilage tumor derived from sclerotome
A cyst lined by endodermal epithelium
A tumor arising from notochord remnants
A tumor derived from neural crest cells
advancedTest.explain: Brachyury marks notochordal lineage, so this is a chordoma. Brachyury staining separates it from chondrosarcoma.

lessons.title: Left-Right Asymmetry: Nodal Cilia and Situs Defects

levels.kid:
Look at yourself in a mirror. Your outside looks almost the same on both sides. But inside, you are not! Your heart leans to the left. Your liver sits on the right. Your stomach curls to the left.

How does a tiny baby know left from right? Very early, there is a small pit in the baby called the **node**. Inside it are tiny hairs called **cilia**. They spin like little propellers, all in the same direction.

Their spinning makes the fluid flow to the left side. That flow is like a signal that says, "This side is left!"

If the hairs don't spin, the body may guess. Sometimes organs end up flipped, like a mirror picture.
levels.hs:
On the outside we look roughly symmetrical, but our organs are arranged asymmetrically. The heart points left, the liver is mostly on the right, the left lung has two lobes and the right has three. This normal arrangement is called **situs solitus**.

The left-right decision is made during gastrulation, around day 15 to 18. At the front of the primitive streak is the **primitive node**. Its pit is lined with cells that each carry one motile **cilium**. These cilia spin clockwise (viewed from above) and are tilted toward the posterior, so together they push fluid leftward. This is called **nodal flow**.

Cells at the edge of the node sense the flow. This switches on a signaling gene called **NODAL** on the left side only. A gene called **PITX2** then tells left-side tissues to develop as "left."

When this fails, you get **situs defects**:
- **Situs inversus totalis**: a complete mirror image. It is often harmless because the organs still connect properly.
- **Heterotaxy**: organs are mixed up, neither normal nor mirrored. It often comes with serious heart defects.

A real example is **primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome)**. The cilia cannot beat properly, so mucus isn't cleared from the airways. About half of affected people have situs inversus, because without nodal flow, sidedness is left to chance.
levels.college:
Left-right (L-R) patterning happens in three steps: symmetry breaking, transfer of the signal to the lateral plate, and organ-specific asymmetric shaping.

**1. Symmetry breaking at the node.** The pit-like ventral node (the human primitive node, equivalent to the mouse ventral node) carries pit cells with single motile monocilia. Unlike 9+2 airway cilia, these have a 9+0 axoneme but still contain dynein arms. They rotate clockwise when viewed from the ventral side. Because their basal bodies sit at the posterior side of each cell, the cilia are tilted posteriorly. The leftward stroke runs far from the cell surface and the return stroke runs close to it, so the result is net leftward flow.

**2. Sensing and transfer.** Crown (perinodal) cells carry immotile cilia containing **PKD2 (polycystin-2)**, a Ca2+ channel. Left-sided flow lowers expression of the NODAL antagonist **DAND5 (Cerl2)** on the left. This frees NODAL activity on that side. The signal then reaches the **left lateral plate mesoderm**, where NODAL induces itself, its feedback inhibitor **LEFTY2**, and the transcription factor **PITX2**.

**3. The midline barrier.** **LEFTY1** in the midline (floor plate and notochord region) keeps NODAL from crossing to the right side.

**Organ outcomes.** PITX2 directs rightward heart looping (D-loop), gut rotation, spleen placement and lung lobation.

**Clinical spectrum:**
- **Situs solitus**: normal arrangement.
- **Situs inversus totalis**: mirror image, with heart defects in only a few percent of cases.
- **Heterotaxy**:
  - Right isomerism (asplenia), with severe complex congenital heart disease.
  - Left isomerism (polysplenia), often with interrupted IVC and azygos continuation.
- **Dextrocardia** alone with normal abdominal situs, which carries a high rate of heart defects.
levels.phd:
The fluid-flow model rests on Nonaka et al. (1998). They showed that mice lacking the kinesin KIF3B have no nodal cilia and randomized situs. Nonaka et al. (2002) then reversed laterality by imposing rightward artificial flow on cultured embryos, which showed that flow is sufficient. The *iv* mouse, carrying a mutation in left-right dynein (**Dnah11**), has immotile nodal cilia and 50% situs inversus: randomization, not reversal. The *inv* mutant (Invs) instead shows near-total reversal. This is classically attributed to abnormal flow, although inversin's role in Wnt/PCP and ciliary compartments complicates that view.

The chirality originates in the cilium itself. Clockwise rotation reflects the molecular handedness of dynein-microtubule assembly. Posterior tilt depends on planar cell polarity (Vangl1/2, Dvl), which places basal bodies posteriorly. Converting rotation into directional flow depends on this tilt and on the low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics near the cell surface.

How flow is sensed remains disputed:
- **Mechanosensory model**: immotile crown-cell cilia bearing PKD2 sense the flow directly. Yoshiba et al. (2012) showed PKD2 is needed in crown cells.
- **Morphogen model**: flow carries signals to the left. Tanaka et al. (2005) described FGF-triggered "nodal vesicular parcels" carrying Shh and retinoic acid.
- **Direct-force evidence**: Djenoune et al. (2023, zebrafish Kupffer's vesicle) and Katoh et al. (2023, mouse) supported cilium bending. Mouse crown-cell cilia respond to the direction of bending, with intraciliary Ca2+ signals.

Downstream, flow degrades Dand5 mRNA on the left in a Bicc1/Ccr4-dependent manner. NODAL-GDF1 heterodimers then act through ALK4/7 and Cripto to SMAD2/3-FOXH1, driving a self-enhancing, long-range lateral plate cascade. The circuit fits a Turing-type reaction-diffusion pattern: NODAL is short-range and LEFTY is long-range, which sharpens the signal into a left-only domain. PITX2c sustains left identity in organ primordia.

Cilia are not universal. Chicks and pigs have no motile nodal cilia, and in chick H+/K+-ATPase-driven gene asymmetry and asymmetric cell movements around Hensen's node break symmetry. In Xenopus, an early ion-flux (Levin) model competes with the gastrocoel roof plate cilia model. Whether human embryos use flow is inferred mainly from PCD genetics.
levels.expert:
Heterotaxy accounts for about 3% of congenital heart disease and causes a disproportionate share of its deaths. Clinicians now favor sequential segmental analysis (Van Praagh, Anderson) over labels like "asplenia/polysplenia." This means describing atrial arrangement by atrial appendage morphology, ventriculoarterial connections, and systemic and pulmonary venous return. Spleen status poorly predicts cardiac anatomy, so each patient needs individual imaging.

**Genetics.** Fewer than a quarter of heterotaxy cases receive a molecular diagnosis. Implicated genes include ZIC3 (X-linked), NODAL, CFC1, LEFTY2, ACVR2B, GDF1, MMP21, CIROP and PKD1L1. MMP21 and CIROP act specifically in L-R patterning without causing airway disease. PCD (DNAH5, DNAI1, CCDC39/40, and others) causes situs inversus in about half of patients and heterotaxy in roughly 6-12%. Exome sequencing of large CHD cohorts (the Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium) found an excess of de novo and recessive cilia-gene variants. Ciliary genes contribute to CHD well beyond classic heterotaxy.

**Practical pitfalls:**
- Right isomerism carries the risk of asplenia and overwhelming encapsulated-organism sepsis. These patients need antibiotic prophylaxis and vaccinations, and a peripheral blood smear for Howell-Jolly bodies plus imaging should confirm splenic status.
- **Intestinal malrotation** occurs often in heterotaxy. Whether to screen and do prophylactic Ladd procedures in asymptomatic children is debated, so many centers now use watchful waiting.
- Neonates with situs inversus and unexplained respiratory distress should be evaluated for PCD (nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy, electron microscopy, genetics). Normal EM ultrastructure does not exclude PCD, because about 30% of genotypes (such as DNAH11) look normal.
- For a neurosurgeon, situs inversus matters for positioning, ECG lead placement and laterality marking. It is a classic setup for wrong-side errors, even though brain lateralization is largely independent. Most people with situs inversus totalis remain left-hemisphere dominant for language, which suggests brain asymmetry uses partly separate pathways.

**Open questions** include how the human node functions (it is rarely studied directly), the stochastic penetrance seen in discordant monozygotic twins, and the higher incidence of laterality defects in conjoined twins and in maternal diabetes.

keyPoints: Normal organ arrangement (situs solitus) is set during gastrulation at the primitive node
Clockwise-rotating, posteriorly tilted nodal cilia create leftward nodal flow
Crown cells sense flow via PKD2 and reduce DAND5, freeing NODAL on the left
NODAL, LEFTY2 and PITX2 specify the left lateral plate; midline LEFTY1 acts as a barrier
Immotile cilia randomize situs: about 50% of PCD patients have situs inversus
Heterotaxy (right or left isomerism) carries complex heart disease and spleen problems

test.q: Where is left-right symmetry first broken in the mammalian embryo?
test.explain: Ciliated pit cells of the primitive (ventral) node generate the leftward flow that breaks symmetry.

test.q: Which direction does nodal flow move the extraembryonic fluid?
test.explain: Rotating, posteriorly tilted cilia produce net leftward flow.

test.q: Why does ciliary rotation produce flow in one direction rather than a whirlpool?
choices: The cilia beat in a whip-like planar stroke
The node cavity is open on the right side
Fluid enters the node from the yolk sac
The cilia are tilted toward the posterior
test.explain: Posterior tilt makes the leftward stroke run away from the cell surface and the return stroke run near it, so the net flow is leftward.

test.q: Which transcription factor carries left identity into organs such as the heart and gut?
test.explain: NODAL induces PITX2 in the left lateral plate mesoderm, and PITX2 directs asymmetric organ shaping.

test.q: What is the role of LEFTY1 in the midline?
choices: It blocks NODAL from crossing to the right
It amplifies NODAL on both sides
It moves cilia into a posterior tilt
test.explain: Midline LEFTY1 acts as a barrier that confines NODAL signaling to the left.

test.q: Roughly what fraction of people with primary ciliary dyskinesia have situs inversus?
test.explain: Without nodal flow, sidedness is random, so about half have situs inversus.

test.q: Which arrangement usually carries the lowest risk of heart defects?
test.explain: A full mirror image preserves normal connections. Heterotaxy and isolated dextrocardia carry high rates of heart defects.

test.q: Right isomerism is classically associated with:
test.explain: Right isomerism means bilateral right-sidedness, which brings asplenia and severe heart disease. Polysplenia goes with left isomerism.

test.q: How does nodal flow increase NODAL activity on the left?
choices: It silences PITX2 on the right side
It lowers the antagonist DAND5 on the left
It raises LEFTY1 in the left lateral plate
It carries NODAL protein from the right
test.explain: Flow sensed by crown cells reduces DAND5 (Cerl2) on the left, releasing NODAL activity there.

test.q: A mixed-up organ arrangement that is neither normal nor a mirror image is called ___.
test.explain: Heterotaxy includes right and left isomerism and is often linked to complex heart disease.

test.q: What calcium channel protein in crown-cell cilia is needed to sense nodal flow?
test.explain: PKD2 (polycystin-2) in the immotile crown-cell cilia is required for sensing flow.

test.q: Situs inversus with chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis is called ___ syndrome.
test.explain: Kartagener syndrome is the subset of primary ciliary dyskinesia that includes situs inversus.

kidTest.q: Which side does your heart lean toward?
kidTest.explain: Your heart points to the left.

kidTest.q: What are the tiny spinning hairs in the node called?
kidTest.explain: Cilia are tiny hairs that spin like propellers.

kidTest.q: Which way do the spinning hairs push the fluid?
kidTest.explain: The fluid flows left, which tells the body where left is.

kidTest.q: What can happen if the tiny hairs don't spin?
kidTest.explain: Without the signal, organs may be mirror-flipped.

kidTest.q: The small pit where the hairs spin is called the n _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The node is where left and right get decided.

advancedTest.q: Dnah11 (iv) mutants show 50% situs inversus, while inv mutants show near-total reversal. What does this contrast suggest?
choices: Situs is set by maternal factors whatever the cilia are doing
Missing flow randomizes situs, while abnormal signaling can bias it
Inversin is needed to assemble the 9+0 axoneme of nodal cilia
Dynein mutations reliably reverse the NODAL cascade in embryos
advancedTest.explain: Immotile cilia remove the cue and leave a coin toss. Reversal implies a directional, though abnormal, signal.

advancedTest.q: Rightward artificial flow imposed on cultured wild-type mouse embryos reverses laterality. This shows that flow is:
choices: Enough to set direction, overriding cilia chirality
Necessary but not enough to orient the embryo
Sensed solely through vesicles carrying Shh
Unrelated to the downstream NODAL response
advancedTest.explain: Nonaka et al. (2002) showed that the direction of imposed flow dictates sidedness, so flow is sufficient.

advancedTest.q: Chick embryos lack motile nodal cilia yet show normal left-right asymmetry. The best interpretation is:
choices: The NODAL-PITX2 cascade is absent in birds
Chicks rely on maternal mRNA placed on one side of the egg
Symmetry breaking can use cilia-independent mechanisms
Chick asymmetry is random, as in PCD
advancedTest.explain: In chick, ion pumps and asymmetric cell movements around Hensen's node break symmetry, while the downstream NODAL-PITX2 cascade is conserved.

advancedTest.q: Why do clinicians favor sequential segmental analysis over asplenia/polysplenia labels in heterotaxy?
choices: Spleen status poorly predicts each heart's anatomy
Isomerism is diagnosed by genetic testing alone
Polysplenia is benign and needs no further workup
Spleen imaging is rarely feasible in newborn infants
advancedTest.explain: Cardiac anatomy varies widely within each spleen category, so each segment must be described directly.

lessons.title: Cephalocaudal and Lateral Folding of the Embryo

levels.kid:
Imagine a flat pancake lying on top of a little balloon. That pancake is the baby at about three weeks old. To become a baby shape, it has to curl up.

First, the head end and the tail end bend down, like a caterpillar curling. Then the two sides roll down and under, like wrapping a burrito. When the edges meet underneath, the flat pancake becomes a tube shape.

The top layer now covers the outside like skin. The bottom layer gets tucked inside and becomes the tummy tube, called the gut. The little balloon gets squeezed into a thin stalk. That stalk helps make the belly button cord.

Folding happens because the brain part grows very fast and pushes the head forward and down.
levels.hs:
During week 4 the flat, three-layer embryonic disc turns into a curved, roughly cylindrical body. This change is called **embryonic folding**, and it happens in two directions at once.

- **Cephalocaudal (head-to-tail) folding**: the head and tail ends curl down toward the yolk sac. It is driven mainly by rapid growth of the brain and spinal cord.
- **Lateral folding**: the right and left edges of the disc roll down and toward the midline, then meet on the underside.

Folding has big results:
- The **ectoderm** ends up covering the whole outside of the embryo.
- Part of the yolk sac, lined by **endoderm**, gets pinched inside to form the **primitive gut**, divided into **foregut**, **midgut** and **hindgut**.
- The midgut stays connected to the shrinking yolk sac by the **vitelline duct**, which normally disappears.
- A space inside the body wall, the **intraembryonic coelom**, becomes the body cavities.
- The **heart** and the **septum transversum** (a future part of the diaphragm) swing from in front of the head to the chest.
- The edges meet at the **umbilical ring**, where the connecting stalk and yolk stalk form the **umbilical cord**.

Real example: if the side folds fail to close properly, a baby can be born with abdominal organs outside the body, as in **gastroschisis** or **omphalocele**.
levels.college:
Folding converts the trilaminar disc into a C-shaped tube within a tube between roughly days 22 and 28. The engine is **differential growth**: the neural tube and somites grow fast while the amnion expands, but the yolk sac grows little. The disc bulges into the amniotic cavity, and its edges curl ventrally.

**Cephalocaudal folding**
- **Cranial fold**: the growing forebrain projects over the **oropharyngeal membrane**. The cardiogenic area and **septum transversum**, which lay cranial to that membrane, rotate about 180° to sit ventral to the foregut, in the future thorax. The septum transversum later contributes to the central tendon of the diaphragm and lies close to the developing liver.
- **Caudal fold**: the **cloacal membrane** and the connecting stalk move ventrally. The **allantois**, a diverticulum of the yolk sac, gets partly drawn into the embryo.
- The pockets of endoderm created are the **foregut** (cranial), ending at the oropharyngeal membrane, and the **hindgut** (caudal), ending at the cloacal membrane.

**Lateral folding**
- **Lateral plate mesoderm** splits into **somatic** (parietal) and **splanchnic** (visceral) layers around the intraembryonic coelom.
- **Somatopleure** (ectoderm plus somatic mesoderm) forms the ventral and lateral body wall.
- **Splanchnopleure** (endoderm plus splanchnic mesoderm) forms the gut wall.
- The folds fuse in the ventral midline, except at the umbilicus. The **midgut** stays in broad contact with the yolk sac via the **vitelline duct**.

**Consequences**
- The coelom is separated from the extraembryonic coelom, leaving a single cavity that the septum transversum and the pleuroperitoneal membranes later divide.
- The **dorsal mesentery** suspends the gut from the posterior body wall.
- The amnion now surrounds the embryo, and the **umbilical cord** forms.

Failure of ventral body wall closure produces **ectopia cordis**, **omphalocele**, **gastroschisis** or **bladder exstrophy**, depending on which part of the closure fails.
levels.phd:
Folding is a mechanically driven morphogenesis. Most data come from chick and mouse, since human week 4 is studied mainly through fixed collections such as the Carnegie series (stages 10-13).

**Drivers.** The classic explanation is that differential proliferation bends the disc: the neural plate and paraxial mesoderm grow quickly while the extraembryonic tissues lag. Other forces add to this:
- **Apical constriction** and cell shape changes in the ventral endoderm and splanchnic mesoderm.
- Tension from the expanding amnion.
- Convergent extension of the axis.

In chick, the **anterior intestinal portal** forms as the foregut pocket deepens. It moves caudally through directed cell movement and regulated cell death. The caudal intestinal portal makes the hindgut by a mirror process.

**Molecular inputs.**
- **Bmp4** from the lateral plate and extraembryonic tissue helps specify ventral body wall and septum transversum fates.
- **Gata4** in splanchnic mesoderm and endoderm is required for ventral closure. Gata4-null mice fail ventral folding and develop **cardia bifida**, two separate heart tubes. Foxa2 and Sox17 mutants also show foregut and heart tube defects, linking endoderm integrity to cardiac fusion.
- Retinoic acid and Wnt gradients bias proliferation along the axis.

**Rotation of the cardiogenic field.** The heart fields form a crescent cranial to the prechordal plate. Head-fold flexion swings them caudoventrally. Lateral folding then brings the paired endocardial tubes to the midline, where they fuse. Cardia bifida is a classic readout of a folding defect rather than a primary heart defect.

**Body wall closure.** Debate continues over whether **omphalocele** and **gastroschisis** share a cause. Omphalocele, which has a membrane covering and is linked to trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, is classically attributed to failed return of the physiological midgut herniation, possibly with a ventral fold defect. Gastroschisis, usually right-sided with no sac, has been explained by competing models:
- Vascular disruption involving the right umbilical vein or the vitelline artery.
- Rupture of the umbilical ring.
- Abnormal incorporation of the yolk sac.

Feinberg and colleagues argued that a failed ventral fold underlies the pentalogy of Cantrell.
levels.expert:
Clinically, folding errors appear as **ventral body wall defects** and gut connection remnants, and they matter for prenatal counselling and surgical planning.

**Prenatal distinctions.** Physiological midgut herniation into the cord is normal until about 11-12 weeks. A diagnosis of omphalocele therefore needs care before then. Ultrasound features that separate the two main defects:
- **Omphalocele**: a sac covers the defect, the cord inserts on the sac, and the liver is often herniated.
- **Gastroschisis**: free-floating bowel, typically to the right of a normally inserted cord.

Gastroschisis incidence rose worldwide over recent decades. It is most strongly linked to young maternal age, and smoking and vasoactive exposures have been studied as risk factors. Omphalocele warrants karyotype or microarray testing and an echocardiogram. Isolated gastroschisis rarely has an aneuploidy.

**Spectrum disorders.**
- **Pentalogy of Cantrell**: a supraumbilical defect, a sternal cleft, an anterior diaphragm defect, a pericardial defect and intracardiac anomalies. This combination maps onto failed cranial and septum transversum folding.
- **OEIS complex** (omphalocele, cloacal exstrophy, imperforate anus, spinal defects) and **bladder exstrophy** reflect caudal fold and cloacal membrane errors.
- **Limb-body wall complex** is a severe, often lethal, combination of disruptions.

**Vitelline remnants.** A **Meckel diverticulum** is the persistent proximal vitelline duct. It is found in about 2% of people and usually lies on the antimesenteric ileum. It may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue, which can cause bleeding, intussusception or volvulus. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy detects ectopic gastric mucosa. Other remnants include umbilical fistulas, cysts and fibrous bands.

**Surgical relevance.** Gastroschisis is managed by primary closure or silo-staged reduction. Giant omphalocele may be treated with "paint and wait" epithelialization followed by delayed closure. In gastroschisis, intestinal dysmotility, not the defect itself, drives long hospital stays.

**Neurosurgical link.** Head-fold flexion and the cephalic flexures relate to how the neural tube bends.

**Open questions.** The cause of gastroschisis remains unresolved. Human embryo culture past gastrulation and stem cell models of the post-gastrulation embryo are starting to reproduce aspects of folding in vitro. These models raise ethical questions under the 14-day rule debates.

keyPoints: Folding in week 4 turns the flat disc into a curved tube-within-a-tube
Rapid neural tube growth drives cephalocaudal folding
Lateral folds meet ventrally, leaving the umbilical ring open
Endoderm pinches in to form foregut, midgut and hindgut
The heart and septum transversum swing from cranial to the thorax
Fold failures cause omphalocele, gastroschisis, ectopia cordis and exstrophy

test.q: During which week does embryonic folding mainly occur?
test.explain: Folding happens around days 22-28, in week 4, just after gastrulation.

test.q: What mainly drives cephalocaudal folding?
choices: Fast growth of the neural tube
test.explain: The neural tube and brain grow fast while the yolk sac lags, so the ends of the disc curl down.

test.q: After folding, which germ layer covers the outside of the embryo?
test.explain: Folding wraps the ectoderm around the whole embryo. The endoderm is tucked inside as the gut.

test.q: Where does the heart end up as a result of head folding?
choices: Ventral to the foregut, in the chest
Inside the yolk sac, outside the body
Dorsal to the neural tube, in the back
Cranial to the brain, near the forehead
test.explain: The cardiogenic area swings about 180° from cranial to the oropharyngeal membrane to a position ventral to the foregut.

test.q: Which structure keeps the midgut connected to the yolk sac?
test.explain: The vitelline (yolk) duct links midgut and yolk sac. The allantois is a caudal diverticulum instead.

test.q: Which membrane marks the cranial end of the foregut?
test.explain: The oropharyngeal membrane closes the foregut cranially. The cloacal membrane closes the hindgut caudally.

test.q: Somatopleure, made of ectoderm plus somatic mesoderm, forms the:
test.explain: Somatopleure forms the ventrolateral body wall. Splanchnopleure, made of endoderm plus splanchnic mesoderm, forms the gut wall.

test.q: Which defect has bowel outside the body with no covering sac, usually right of the cord?
test.explain: Gastroschisis has no sac and the cord inserts normally. Omphalocele has a covering membrane.

test.q: The septum transversum later contributes to the:
test.explain: The septum transversum forms part of the central tendon of the diaphragm.

test.q: The endoderm-lined tube formed by folding is divided into foregut, ___ and hindgut.
test.explain: The primitive gut has three parts, and the midgut stays open to the yolk sac.

test.q: What is the space inside the lateral plate mesoderm that becomes the body cavities called?
test.explain: The intraembryonic coelom separates the somatic and splanchnic layers and later becomes the pericardial, pleural and peritoneal cavities.

test.q: The lateral folds meet ventrally except at the ___ ring, where the cord attaches.
test.explain: The umbilical ring is where the connecting stalk and yolk stalk exit to form the cord.

kidTest.q: At first, what shape is the tiny baby before folding?
kidTest.explain: It starts flat, like a pancake, and then curls up.

kidTest.q: What do the sides of the disc do when they fold?
kidTest.explain: Like wrapping a burrito, the sides roll under and meet.

kidTest.q: What does the inside layer become?
kidTest.explain: The inside layer becomes the gut, the tube in your tummy.

kidTest.q: Which part grows fast and pushes the head forward?
kidTest.explain: The brain grows very quickly and helps curl the head down.

kidTest.q: The squeezed stalk helps make the belly button ___ (c _ _ _).
kidTest.explain: It becomes part of the umbilical cord.

advancedTest.q: Gata4-null mice develop cardia bifida. What does this best indicate?
choices: Cardiomyocytes fail to differentiate from mesoderm
Failed ventral folding stops the heart tubes from meeting
The neural tube fails to close at its cranial end
The left-right axis is fully reversed in these mice
advancedTest.explain: The paired heart tubes need lateral folding to bring them to the midline. Cardia bifida reflects a folding defect, not a lack of heart muscle.

advancedTest.q: A 10-week scan shows bowel in the cord base. What is the most appropriate reasoning?
choices: Consider physiological herniation and rescan later
Diagnose gastroschisis because no sac is visible yet
Suspect a Meckel diverticulum from vitelline duct remnants
Confirm omphalocele and order a karyotype at once
advancedTest.explain: Physiological midgut herniation is normal until about 11-12 weeks, so diagnosing omphalocele this early is premature.

advancedTest.q: Which pairing best links a folding failure to its defect?
choices: Caudal fold failure with pentalogy of Cantrell
Cranial fold failure with ectopia cordis
Lateral fold failure with Meckel diverticulum
Cranial fold failure with bladder exstrophy
advancedTest.explain: Ectopia cordis and Cantrell's pentalogy reflect cranial and septum transversum defects. Exstrophy is caudal, and Meckel comes from a persistent vitelline duct.

advancedTest.q: Why does omphalocele call for genetic testing more than gastroschisis does?
choices: Omphalocele results from maternal smoking in most cases
Gastroschisis is caused by a single known gene mutation
Gastroschisis is detected after birth rather than on ultrasound
Omphalocele is strongly linked to aneuploidy and syndromes
advancedTest.explain: Omphalocele is associated with trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Isolated gastroschisis is rarely aneuploid and has no single known gene cause.
